subtitulo: A look at its geological wonders
lema: “Geositios de Chile: una mirada a sus maravillas geológicas” (Geosites of Chile: A Look at Its Geological Wonders) is a book that seeks to share the extraordinary geological diversity and richness of our country. Geosites are small chapters of the vast and fascinating natural history of Chile and the planet. They are our heritage, and they must also be our legacy.
pie_portada: view to the northwest of the Cerro Castillo geosite. The rock wall shows the different geological units that make it up, partly covered by snowfields or sediment. At the bottom, a glacial lake. Photo: Felipe Andrade A.

prologos.titulo: Foreword by the National Director of Sernageomin, Patricio Aguilera Poblete
prologos.texto: An important part of our mission as the National Geology and Mining Service is to generate, maintain and disseminate information on basic geology and on the geological resources and hazards of the national territory, serving the country's development and the well-being and safety of the community. That is why this book, which describes and organizes part of our geological heritage, is consistent with our institutional mission. “Geosites of Chile, a look at its geological wonders” was born from the interest, effort and vision of Sernageomin's professionals to share with society the extraordinary geological diversity and richness of our country. Going through these pages and exploring each of the 49 geosites described will give us a new look at geological phenomena that have shaped and configured our territory, representing various processes that occurred during its geological evolution, from the Paleozoic era to the present, including aspects related to the origin and evolution of life on Earth. However, the importance of some of these places is not only due to the geoscientific knowledge we have about them: their links to historical events or ancestral knowledge, their well-known recreational or tourist use, or their role in supporting knowledge of diverse ecosystems throughout our country give them greater relevance and bring them closer to people and communities. We invite everyone to enjoy this book, which offers the chance to know, appreciate and value even more the diversity of our territory, and to raise awareness of how we occupy it and develop within it, especially at this stage of human evolution in which we face significant global changes that are increasingly frequent and severe. Finally, in a task shared with other institutions, above all the prestigious Geological Society of Chile, we hope this book will contribute to the recognition of these and other places relevant to the geosciences, which belong to the diverse and vast natural heritage of our country, and that it will therefore also help generate and activate the conservation measures they deserve.

prologos.titulo: Foreword by the President of the Geological Society of Chile, Millarca Valenzuela Picón
prologos.texto: “Geosites of Chile, a look at its geological wonders” arrives at a critical moment for Chile, in the year when many families lost their homes, built in flood zones that had been dry for many years, along almost every river in south-central Chile, and with the shocking case of the sinkholes in the Concón Dunes, one of the geosites in this book. The climate crisis is already here, hitting us hard with material damage and loss of life that could be avoided if the whole chain of public and private institutions responsible for building understood that territories at high risk of disaster should not be used for that purpose, as technical agencies such as Sernageomin advise. These cases lead us to reflect that we need political leaders, business people and state officials who better understand the aspects of geoscience that affect society, and also citizens who know the territories they inhabit so they can live in them more safely. During my work in Sernageomin's Geoheritage Unit in 2018, I was in charge of the first steps toward this book, conceived as one of the first tasks under the framework agreement signed between Sernageomin and the Geological Society of Chile to collaborate on the geoheritage issues both institutions share. The aim was a book that would help spread the geological richness of the country, with emblematic sites that citizens could identify with (Morro de Arica, Cerro Dragón Dune, La Portada and others), but also more remote ones, to make them known and show how these places can tell small or great stories of planet Earth. The synoptic map of the geosites on the geological time chart included in the book, together with the geological context in which they all appear, offers a pleasant way to discover the stories each one tells, which in turn helps us better understand the geology of the places where we live, which have undergone incredible processes and transformations, leaving traces that we must then decipher. I invite you to enjoy and marvel at these magnificent representatives of the more than 500 geosites currently in the repositories of Sernageomin, the Geological Society of Chile and other institutions, which we hope will keep growing and raising awareness of the territory that nourishes our lives, so that we can enjoy it and also make better decisions about how to live in it.

parrafos: The Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite lies just over 7.8 km west of the village of Ancuta, in Parinacota Province. The most direct way to reach it, however, is to head south from kilometer 158 of international route CH-11 (12 km before Chucuyo), along route A-235 to Misitune, and then continue south on route A-245 to about 1.5 km before the junction with route A-243, where a turn-off leads closer to the geosite.

This geosite is an amphitheater-shaped section of the valley where, from the Pleistocene to the present, erosion has sculpted striking pillar-like structures. They formed through intense runoff over slopes made of a series of lake sediment layers of varying thickness and different shades of brown, interbedded with whitish layers of volcanic ash. This whole sequence of sediments and ash is grouped into the so-called Lauca Formation, dated between 6.2 and 2.6 million years ago, spanning the Late Miocene to Late Pliocene.
pies: Top: view west of the village of Ancuta near the Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite, Arica y Parinacota Region. Bottom: the Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite. On the right, brown and ochre layers of lake sediments and whiter layers of volcanic ash. In the background, among clouds, Guallatiri volcano. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.

parrafos: The Morro de Arica geosite is a coastal hill about 280 m high at the southern end of the city of Arica. Declared a National Monument on October 6, 1971, it marks the northern end of the Coastal Range in Chile and the beginning of the coastal cliff. Its rocks, assigned to the Camaraca Formation, are the oldest in Arica Province and, based on their fossils, date to the Middle Jurassic, roughly 170 to 163 million years ago.

The cliff, the result of uplift and erosion during the Pleistocene to the present, exposes a sequence of layers gently tilted to the east (15-20°), made up mainly of andesitic lavas interbedded with fossil-bearing marine sedimentary rocks. The whole sequence formed in a shallow marine environment, as shown by its fossils: bivalves, ammonites, echinoderms, corals and brachiopods, all marine organisms of shallow waters.

The source of the volcanic material lay close to the coast, as shown by rapid-cooling structures formed when the lava came into contact with seawater. Lavas with these structures are called pillow lavas because of their oval shapes, and they can be seen with the naked eye in the rocks of the Morro.
This geosite is the main symbol of the city and is visited by many tourists every year, both for its panoramic view of the city and nearby beaches and for its historical significance.
pies: View north-northeast of the city of Arica from the Morro de Arica geosite. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.
Top: general view south of the Morro de Arica. Source: © Photographic Archive of the National Monuments Council, 2008. Photo: Karina Sánchez V.
Bottom: pillow lava structures in the middle of the western slope of the Morro de Arica, notable for their rough texture and oval shapes. Photo: Guillermo López A., Sernageomin.

parrafos: The Amuyo lagoons, near the village of Camiña, are the surface expression of a deep hydrothermal system in which high-temperature fluids circulate through highly permeable volcanic rocks of the Oxaya Formation, of Oligocene-Miocene age. This circulation dissolves certain minerals in those rocks and increases the salinity and the concentration of some elements and compounds in the fluids.

The rise of these fluids and the constant precipitation of salts during the Middle Miocene to the present have formed hot-spring rocks: thick crusts of very striking colors that give the lagoons their name. Depending on the fluid composition, the crusts can be yellowish-green, if rich in the mineral orpiment, or orange-red, if realgar is abundant. The continuous build-up of crusts has formed a dome about 400 m across that rises some 15 m above the Caritaya River.

These extreme and unique environments also host bacterial colonies that tolerate the lagoons' high temperatures and salt concentrations (the Red Lagoon reaches a maximum of 57 °C measured at 11 m depth). These bacterial communities, called thermophiles because of their tolerance to heat, build organic structures known as stromatolites and thrombolites. Since such organisms have existed on Earth for about 3,500 million years, studying the colonies at this geosite is key to understanding the origin and development of life on Earth and the possibility of extraterrestrial life.

Because of the unusual colors of their waters and deposits, their striking shape and their contrast with the dull surroundings, these lagoons are a ritual space for Indigenous communities, which has given rise to rich stories and imagery about them, and they are also a major local tourist attraction.
pies: Top: view east of the red lagoon of Amuyo, Arica y Parinacota Region. Bottom: view east of the red lagoon, showing the salt crusts of different colors that give the lagoons of this geosite their hues. Photo: Francisco Munita Y.

parrafos: The Cerro Dragón dune, declared a Nature Sanctuary in 2005, is one of the most important and striking landforms in the arid landscapes of northern Chile. This coastal dune sits at the southern end of a narrow, rocky marine terrace, averaging about 52 m a.s.l., bounded to the east by a coastal cliff some 500 m high, and on which the city of Iquique has developed.

About 4 km long and between 150 and 550 m wide, it stands out for its sharp, elongated and winding summit ending in a high, pointed crest. These features are precisely what make it look like a reclining dragon. Today the dune has no active source of sand, such as a beach, so it is classified as fossil or relict.

It has been proposed that it originated during the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago in the Late Pleistocene, when sea level was some 100 m lower than today and exposed a platform about 5 km wide, whose sediments would have supplied the sand to build the dune.

Despite being a protected area, the urban growth of Iquique has endangered the integrity and very existence of the Cerro Dragón dune. Real-estate pressure, sand extraction for construction and recreational activities have fragmented the dune and degraded its original natural landforms.
pies: Top: view northwest of the Cerro Dragón Dune and the city of Iquique. Bottom: view south of the dune, with its sharp, winding crest in the center; on the left, the imposing coastal cliff about 500 m high, and on the right, Iquique on the coastal platform. Photo: Natalia Espina L., Sernageomin.

parrafos: The Pintados salt flat, 47 km south of Pozo Almonte, lies within the Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve, created in 1988. It is located where the Central Depression meets the Coastal Range, at the northern end of the Pampa del Tamarugal. It is a fossil or inactive salt flat, since it receives no recharge from surface streams, and its age spans the Pleistocene-Holocene, from about 2.6 million years ago to the present.

The salt flat is made of salt crusts and minor amounts of fine sediment. The most common salts are sulfates (gypsum, anhydrite), carbonates, nitrates and halides (common salt), forming a surface crust disconnected from the deep groundwater. Chemical analyses of this groundwater show a predominance of sulfates and sodium, although in some areas chloride or bicarbonate, and magnesium or calcium, also prevail, especially toward the southwest of the salt flat.

On the eastern slopes of the Coastal Range, in the central-western part of the salt flat, are the Pintados geoglyphs, declared a Historic Monument in 1969. They include about 450 figures over 50,000 m2 along a 3 km stretch. They were made by pre-Hispanic peoples between 700 and 1500 AD, mostly by removing surface material to create contrast with the natural rock surface.
An interpretation center here provides information about the geoglyphs and the archaeological finds related to the pre-Hispanic peoples.
pies: View west of the rough crust of the Pintados salt flat, with the interpretation center and the slopes bearing the geoglyphs. Photo: Felipe Fuentes C., Sernageomin.
Top: view west of the Pintados geoglyphs.
Bottom: gypsum layer in the salt crust near the interpretation center.
